deep_why: The core problem is measuring whether named things mentioned in search results actually help users find what they want. The soundness rests on a simple principle: if the model learns which named things appear in documents that users already marked as helpful, it gains an unfair head start—it's memorizing the answer instead of learning to recognize it from text alone. This breaks down here because the method leaked information about which entities only appeared in pre-labeled good results, creating circular reasoning in the ranking pipeline. Without truly learning from document content, the system cannot work in the real world where it encounters new queries and documents it has never seen during training, making the approach impractical regardless of benchmark scores.

The goal is to rank search results using the internal thinking patterns of large language models without waiting for them to write out answers, which is computationally expensive. The method works because all transformers—regardless of their specific design—show a consistent pattern: signals indicating which documents matter most build up gradually through the layers, peak in the middle layers, then fade again, like a bell curve. Because this pattern holds across different model architectures, researchers can safely extract only the strong-signal layers and skip the weak early and late ones. This soundness means they can cut inference time in half while keeping ranking quality intact, since the discarded layers weren't carrying useful information anyway.

When recommender systems use graph techniques that work with frequency patterns to separate true user preferences from noise, they should outperform simpler classical methods—but reproducibility reveals this isn't consistent. The underlying principle that makes frequency-based separation sound is that real preference signals should occupy different frequency zones than noise, allowing filtering to preserve one while removing the other. This principle only holds if the frequency separation actually exists and if the method implements it correctly. The study found that implementation errors and metric miscalculations inflated results; when these are fixed and classical baselines are properly tuned, they remain surprisingly competitive, showing that the frequency principle isn't guaranteed to dominate in practice.

Standard search systems score document relevance by multiplying a query's numerical representation with each document's representation—a fixed formula that cannot adapt to what the query is asking. The Hypencoder improves this by building a query-specific scoring function whose settings change based on the query itself, like switching to a specialized tool for each task. This works because a flexible scoring function has more power to express different relevance patterns than a one-size-fits-all formula can achieve; the soundness comes from allowing the model to learn what scoring strategy works best for each distinct query situation. However, reproducibility confirms this gain is real only when the initial encoder is well-trained and the method is fine-tuned carefully, meaning the principle's benefit depends heavily on execution.

Multi-vector retrieval models break each document and query into several small numerical chunks and match them separately to find relevant results. The method's weakness lies in its fundamental design: it uses a uniform weighting scheme where all chunks contribute equally, which cannot distinguish important information from filler text—for long questions about narratives, short signal gets lost in noise. The mathematical principle underlying the approach assumes equal weighting works, but when document length grows, this assumption breaks; the architecture literally cannot learn to ignore irrelevant filler at scale. This architectural ceiling cannot be overcome by simply adding more training data or tweaking parameters, which is why the system fails on longer, more complex queries.

Search engines retrieve documents by reading an inverted index in different orders—either processing all results for one query at a time, or stopping early once enough high-scoring results accumulate. The soundness of the stop-early approach rests on a guarantee: if you process results in descending order of quality scores, you can safely quit once a score drops below a threshold, knowing no unread results will be better. This principle holds only if scores are calculated consistently and compression techniques don't distort them. The study reveals that different implementations use different compression codecs and indexing methods; when these are unified, previously unexplained performance differences vanish, confirming the principle works once the systems are actually comparable.

Multi-hop question answering requires gathering information from multiple sources, but the system must know when to stop searching—continuing forever wastes computation. The metacognitive approach teaches the model to critique its own understanding and decide whether more information is needed, like a researcher asking whether they have enough evidence before concluding. This works because having the model reflect on what it knows versus what's missing creates a self-correcting loop: poor reasoning becomes visible to the model itself, which can then request more sources. However, reproducibility shows that this principle's power depends on having clear, reliable stopping criteria and good retrieval components; without careful implementation, the self-critique alone cannot fully overcome fundamental limitations in what the underlying components retrieve.

When measuring whether conversational recommender systems work well, researchers use recall metrics that count how many recommended items the user already wanted. The soundness of this measurement breaks when different studies preprocess data differently and when the model can exploit shortcuts—for instance, recommending the same items repeatedly, which technically raises the recall score but fails to have a real conversation. The study reveals that nearly half the reported improvements come from these repetition shortcuts rather than genuine model skill; fine-grained recall metrics are extremely sensitive to implementation choices, making it impossible to fairly compare results across papers. By establishing standardized evaluation, they expose that the underlying principle—that higher recall means better recommendations—only holds when you measure novelty and prevent shortcut exploitation.

Dense search systems compress numerical document representations into smaller approximations to save storage space, using a method that splits representations into chunks and quantizes each chunk separately to nearby cluster centers. The soundness depends on a key guarantee: if each chunk is independently compressed, the recombined compressed representation remains useful for ranking because the relevant matching signals are preserved across chunks. This principle works for older, well-studied models like STAR but fails for newer, larger models like RepLLama, showing that the guarantee only holds when chunks are sufficiently independent—newer models learn dense representations where chunks tightly depend on each other. The replicability study reveals that the method's domain of applicability is narrower than assumed, since the independence assumption breaks with modern architectures.

When search systems receive some irrelevant documents mixed with relevant ones, surprisingly they sometimes answer questions better, supposedly because the noise prevents the model from over-committing to wrong answers. The soundness of this benefit depends on the noise actually being random and disruptive to early wrong paths. However, reproducibility shows this effect is extremely fragile—changing the prompt or removing output length constraints causes the benefit to vanish entirely. The underlying principle assumes the model's errors are due to premature commitment, but error analysis reveals most failures come from truncation or malformed outputs from the language model itself, not from the retrieval input. Without robustness across conditions, the noise effect cannot be trusted as a general principle.

E-commerce recommenders must account for price because users care about cost when deciding purchases—adding price as an explicit feature should improve predictions. The soundness of this approach depends on the architecture capturing how price and preference interact, whether synergistically or through trade-offs. Different methods use different graph structures to represent these interactions: heterogeneous hypergraphs, graph neural networks, and graph convolutional networks. The study shows that heterogeneous hypergraphs (CoHHN) most consistently capture these price-preference relationships across diverse datasets, while simpler graph approaches struggle to generalize. This reveals that architectural choice matters enormously; the principle that adding price helps only translates to robust recommendations when the model's structure can actually learn meaningful price effects.

Generative retrieval ranks documents by generating their identifiers one symbol at a time, using predicted look-ahead signals to guide which symbols to explore—avoiding dead branches early prevents wasting time on irrelevant paths. The soundness of this guidance rests on a straightforward idea: planning ahead should help the generation system stay on track toward good documents by computing which prefixes lead toward relevant outcomes. However, stress-testing reveals the plan is extremely brittle: small variations in query wording like typos or synonym substitutions cause the planning signals to shift unexpectedly, collapsing the guidance's utility. The underlying principle assumes planning is stable across minor surface changes, but this fails because the model is over-fitting to specific query words rather than learning robust query meaning, making the look-ahead prior unreliable in practice.

Explaining recommendations by finding minimal tweaks to user history that flip the recommendation is intuitive: if you change just one user-item interaction and the recommendation changes, that interaction must matter. The soundness rests on a key principle: simpler, smaller explanations (fewer tweaks) are more trustworthy than complex ones, because they isolate the true causal factors. However, this principle only holds if you measure explanations consistently—different studies assess item-level changes, list-level changes, and graph changes differently, making comparison impossible. The benchmarking study establishes unified metrics and finds that previous method comparisons depended heavily on which evaluation format was chosen, showing the principle works only when explanations are measured against the same standard.

Learned sparse retrieval models assign weights to vocabulary words that match queries to documents, claiming interpretability because humans can see which words matter. However, some assigned weights point to words seemingly unrelated to the query—these wacky weights undermine interpretability. The soundness of the whole-model interpretability claim depends on the learned weights actually reflecting semantic relevance. The study systematically investigates what causes wackiness and finds that larger vocabulary dictionaries and weaker sparsity controls lead to more uninterpretable weights, while stricter controls reduce them. This reveals that interpretability is not an inherent property of sparse models but depends critically on design choices; the principle that sparse models are interpretable holds only when trained with tight sparsity constraints and modest vocabulary sizes.

Multi-vector retrieval represents documents using many numerical chunks but only has time to process a subset, so it must prune less important chunks. The soundness of pruning depends on a simple principle: less important chunks carry less information about relevance, so removing them barely hurts ranking quality if you keep the top-scoring ones. Weighted pruning that prioritizes chunks by their learned importance scores should outperform simpler heuristics, but the study finds that very simple fixed-count pruning can work equally well if the model is trained properly. This reveals that the pruning principle's effectiveness depends not on the sophistication of the pruning method itself but on whether the training process gives the model enough information to learn which chunks it can safely depend on even with aggressive pruning.
